global_summary: Explains why CORS and antiforgery solve different browser-security problems: CORS controls cross-origin JavaScript access and some non-simple request delivery, while antiforgery protects cookie-authenticated state-changing endpoints from cross-site request forgery.

regions.title: Attacker capabilities and CORS boundaries
regions.summary: Classic HTML mechanisms such as forms, images and navigation can send cross-origin requests even when JavaScript cannot read responses. CORS is primarily an origin-based browser access-control mechanism; it does not authenticate a request and is not a complete CSRF defense.

regions.title: Simple requests, preflight and why CORS is not enough
regions.summary: Simple requests can be sent without preflight. A cookie-authenticated cross-site form POST may therefore reach the server and change state. Non-simple requests trigger OPTIONS preflight; if preflight fails the browser does not send the actual request, but this behavior must not be treated as antiforgery validation.

regions.title: XHR/fetch behavior and practical defense
regions.summary: XHR and fetch expose CORS failures to JavaScript and support modern API request shapes. Practical defense combines same-site cookie settings, server-side antiforgery tokens for cookie-authenticated unsafe methods, careful CORS allowlists, explicit credentials policy and defense-in-depth headers/origin checks.

reading_quality: High conceptual readability. Screenshots and code examples were readable enough for semantic transcription; preserved PNGs remain source of truth for exact punctuation and code formatting.
